claim: In many bacteria and eukaryotes, replication fork establishment requires the controlled loading of hexameric, ring-shaped helicases around DNA by AAA+ (ATPases Associated with various cellular Activities) ATPases.
source: In many bacteria and eukaryotes, replication fork establishment requires the controlled loading of hexameric, ring-shaped helicases around DNA by AAA+(ATPases Associated with various cellular Activities) ATPases.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about replication mechanisms in bacteria and eukaryotes.

claim: DnaC is an archetypal loader for the bacterial DnaB helicase.
source: Here, we dissect how specific ATPase elements of Escherichia coli DnaC, an archetypal loader for the bacterial DnaB helicase, play distinct roles in helicase loading and the activation of DNA unwinding.
evidence: This is a characterization of DnaC based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: A new element called the arginine-coupler regulates the switch-like behavior of DnaC to prevent futile ATPase cycling and maintains loader responsiveness to replication restart systems.
source: We have identified a new element, the arginine-coupler, which regulates the switch-like behavior of DnaC to prevent futile ATPase cycling and maintains loader responsiveness to replication restart systems.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Elements analogous to the Arg-coupler are present in related, switch-like AAA+ proteins that control replicative helicase loading in eukaryotes, as well as in polymerase clamp loading and certain classes of DNA transposases.
source: Our data help explain how the ATPase cycle of a AAA+-family helicase loader is channeled into productive action on its target; comparative studies indicate that elements analogous to the Arg-coupler are present in related, switch-like AAA+ proteins that control replicative helicase loading in eukaryotes, as well as in polymerase clamp loading and certain classes of DNA transposases.
evidence: This is supported by comparative sequence and structural analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: DnaB proteins form hexameric rings and are generally incapable of spontaneously associating with chromosomal replication start sites (origins).
source: DnaB proteins form hexameric rings and are generally incapable of spontaneously associating with chromosomal replication start sites (origins).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DnaB helicase behavior.

claim: DnaB helicases are specifically recruited and deposited onto single-stranded origin DNA by dedicated initiation and loading factors.
source: As a consequence, DnaB helicases are specifically recruited and deposited onto single-stranded origin DNA by dedicated initiation and loading factors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of DnaB loading.

claim: Replicative helicase loading in bacteria depends on at least one of two known types of proteins: DciA-related proteins (ATP-independent) and DnaC/DnaI-family proteins (ATP-dependent).
source: Replicative helicase loading in bacteria depends on at least one of two known types of proteins. One widespread class, comprising factors related to a protein known as DciA, is ATP-independent (Brézellec et al., 2016; Mann et al., 2017). The second class is composed of DnaC/DnaI-family proteins, which are ATP-dependent and present in model organisms such as E. coli and Bacillus subtilis (B. subtilis) (Brézellec et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Both DnaC and DnaI consist of an N-terminal helicase-binding domain (HBD) fused to a C-terminal AAA+ nucleotide-binding fold.
source: Both DnaC and DnaI consist of an N-terminal helicase-binding domain (HBD) fused to a C-terminal AAA+ (ATPases Associated with various cellular Activities) nucleotide-binding fold (Figure 1A; Ludlam et al., 2001; Neuwald et al., 1999b).
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 1A showing the domain organization.

claim: The AAA+ region of DnaC contains numerous signature sequence motifs (Walker A, Walker B, Sensor I and II, Arginine-finger), several of which have been reported to be critical for the function of the loader in E. coli.
source: The AAA+ region of DnaC contains numerous signature sequence motifs (Walker A, Walker B, Sensor I and II, Arginine-finger), several of which have been reported to be critical for the function of the loader in E. coli (Makowska-Grzyska and Kaguni, 2010; Mott et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: DnaC-type loaders help place DnaB hexamers on single-stranded DNA by opening the helicase ring and allowing a nucleic acid strand to laterally enter into the pore of the complex.
source: DnaC-type loaders help place DnaB hexamers on single-stranded DNA by opening the helicase ring and allowing a nucleic acid strand to laterally enter into the pore of the complex (Arias-Palomo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior structural work.

claim: Six DnaC protomers form a cracked hexameric oligomer, generating composite ATPase active sites at five of the six subunit interfaces.
source: In the context of DnaB, six DnaC protomers form a cracked hexameric oligomer, generating composite ATPase active sites at five of the six subunit interfaces (Figure 1B,C; Arias-Palomo et al., 2013; Arias-Palomo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations and structural data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The AAA+ fold of DnaC binds ssDNA directly, at a site distal from its ATP-binding locus.
source: The AAA+ fold of DnaC binds ssDNA directly, at a site distal from its ATP-binding locus (Arias-Palomo and Berger, 2015; Ioannou et al., 2006; Mott et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Prior to binding DNA, DnaC protomers latch onto a DnaB hexamer through their HBDs to promote helicase ring opening.
source: Prior to binding DNA, DnaC protomers latch onto a DnaB hexamer through their HBDs to promote helicase ring opening.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prior structural studies.

claim: Electron microscopy studies have shown that before DNA binding, DnaB resides in an ADP-like state and DnaC in an ATP-bound form.
source: In this configuration, electron microscopy studies have shown that DnaB resides in an ADP-like state and DnaC in an ATP-bound form (Arias-Palomo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior electron microscopy work.

claim: DNA binding induces a large conformational rearrangement in the DnaB hexamer and compresses the DnaC ATPase ring, switching the ATPase status of the helicase and the loader into ATP and ADP forms, respectively.
source: DNA binding induces a large conformational rearrangement in the DnaB hexamer and compresses the DnaC ATPase ring, switching the ATPase status of the helicase and the loader into ATP and ADP forms, respectively.
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies.

claim: Although DnaB helps promote the local co-association of neighboring DnaC AAA+ domains, the ATPase activity of the loader does not manifest until ssDNA is bound.
source: Curiously, although DnaB helps promote the local co-association of neighboring DnaC AAA+ domains, the ATPase activity of the loader does not manifest until ssDNA is bound (Arias-Palomo et al., 2013; Davey et al., 2002; Kobori and Kornberg, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior biochemical work.

claim: The ablation of any of the five key AAA+ residues (Walker A K112R, Walker B E170Q, Sensor I N203A, Arg-finger R220D, Sensor II R237D) results in the complete loss of ATPase function.
source: The ablation of any of the five residues was found to result in the complete loss of ATPase function (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The AAA+ domain and the ATP-hydrolysis cycle of DnaC increase the efficiency of helicase loading.
source: These results demonstrate that the AAA+ domain and the ATP-hydrolysis cycle of DnaC increase the efficiency of helicase loading.
evidence: This is supported by the loading assay data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: Different AAA+ active site residues contribute to the efficiency of DnaB deposition by varying degrees.
source: They also show that, despite being required for ATPase function overall, different AAA+ active site residues contribute to the efficiency of DnaB deposition by varying degrees.
evidence: This is supported by the loading efficiency data for different mutants shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The ATPase-deficient DnaB (DnaBKAEA) is loaded by DnaC, but at a reduced level (~50%) compared to the wild-type helicase.
source: The resultant data show that the ATPase-deficient DnaB is loaded by DnaC, but at a reduced level (~50%) compared to the wild-type helicase (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A majority of the loaded DnaB remained associated with ssDNA when NaCl was increased from 100 to 250 mM.
source: A majority of the loaded DnaB remained associated with ssDNA when NaCl was increased from 100 to 250 mM (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The ability of DnaB to hydrolyze nucleotides is not critical for loading, but does aid the efficiency of the deposition reaction.
source: These results demonstrate that the ability of DnaB to hydrolyze nucleotides is not critical for loading, but does aid the efficiency of the deposition reaction, and that once loaded, DnaB persists in a salt-stable complex with ssDNA.
evidence: This is supported by the loading data comparing wild-type and ATPase-deficient DnaB.

claim: Once loaded, DnaB persists in a salt-stable complex with ssDNA, indicating that the topologically closed-ring conformation observed structurally for the DnaBC complex on DNA persists in solution.
source: These results demonstrate that the ability of DnaB to hydrolyze nucleotides is not critical for loading, but does aid the efficiency of the deposition reaction, and that once loaded, DnaB persists in a salt-stable complex with ssDNA. This latter finding indicates that the topologically closed-ring conformation observed structurally for the DnaBC complex on DNA persists in solution.
evidence: This is an inference from the salt-stability data combined with prior structural knowledge.

claim: DnaC can unload DnaB in an ATP-dependent manner.
source: The presence of ADP in the column buffer still resulted in efficient DnaB loading. By contrast, the inclusion of ATP led to a near-complete loss of DnaB that remained associated with M13 DNA (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D), demonstrating that DnaC can unload DnaB in an ATP-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The ATPase activity of DnaB is important for its unloading from DNA.
source: Interestingly, substantially more ATPase-deficient DnaB remained loaded on the M13 ssDNA in the presence of ATP compared to wild-type DnaB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–F). This finding shows that the ATPase activity of DnaB is important for its unloading from DNA, as well as for loading.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–F.

claim: DnaC stimulates the unwinding of forked DNA substrates by the helicase.
source: In addition to controlling DnaB loading, DnaC has been shown to stimulate the unwinding of forked DNA substrates by the helicase (Arias-Palomo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: When present at only a twofold molar excess over the forked substrate, DnaB was observed to unwind ~10% of the DNA.
source: When present at only a twofold molar excess over the forked substrate, DnaB was observed to unwind ~10% of the DNA (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Blocking the 3'-end of the fork with a biotin-neutravidin complex resulted in a higher proportion of observed fork unwinding (~45%), but the total amount of unwound product was still less than that seen when DnaC was present (~80%).
source: This block resulted in a higher proportion of observed fork unwinding, but the total amount of unwound product (~45%) was still less than that seen when DnaC was present (~80%) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The level of stimulation afforded by DnaC is comparable whether a 3'-end block is present or not.
source: Interestingly, the level of stimulation afforded by DnaC is comparable whether a 3'-end block is present or not (compare 'B + C' curves in Figure 4A vs. Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of experimental data in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: 3' DNA ends can either sequester a proportion of DnaB or fold back against the duplex in a manner that can allow DnaB to translocate over the three strands without unwinding the substrate.
source: These results indicate that 3' DNA ends can either sequester a proportion of DnaB or fold back against the duplex in a manner that can allow DnaB to translocate over the three strands without unwinding the substrate (Kaplan and O'Donnell, 2004), but that DnaC can overcome such inactive states.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data combined with a citation to prior work.

claim: The isolated HBD of DnaC readily stimulates DnaB activity on an unblocked fork, at a level close to that of the full-length loading factor.
source: As seen previously (Arias-Palomo et al., 2013), the isolated HBD of DnaC readily stimulates DnaB activity on an unblocked fork, at a level close to that of the full-length loading factor (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and a citation to prior work.

claim: The DnaC ATPase mutants were much less capable in their response to stimulating helicase unwinding compared to wild-type DnaC.
source: By comparison, the DnaC ATPase mutants were much less capable in their response (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Walker-A mutant showed ~40–50% the stimulatory activity of wild-type DnaC.
source: For example, the Walker-A mutant showed ~40–50% the stimulatory activity of wild-type DnaC, whereas the charge-reversed Arg-finger mutant failed to stimulate DnaB beyond the basal level of the helicase alone (other mutants were intermediate in their response, with ~25–30% the activity of the native loader).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The charge-reversed Arg-finger mutant failed to stimulate DnaB beyond the basal level of the helicase alone.
source: For example, the Walker-A mutant showed ~40–50% the stimulatory activity of wild-type DnaC, whereas the charge-reversed Arg-finger mutant failed to stimulate DnaB beyond the basal level of the helicase alone (other mutants were intermediate in their response, with ~25–30% the activity of the native loader).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The capacity of adjoining DnaC protomers to interact with one another in a nucleotide-dependent manner can influence the extent to which the loader can stimulate DNA unwinding by DnaB.
source: This behavior suggests that the capacity of adjoining DnaC protomers to interact with one another in a nucleotide-dependent manner can influence the extent to which the loader can stimulate DNA unwinding by DnaB.
evidence: This is an inference from the pattern of mutant activities observed.

claim: Recent structural studies of DnaC bound to DnaB and ssDNA noted three conserved amino acids—Phe146, Ser177, and Tyr179—which associate with the nucleic acid strand.
source: Recent structural studies of DnaC bound to DnaB and ssDNA noted three conserved amino acids—Phe146, Ser177, and Tyr179—which associate with the nucleic acid strand (Figures 1 and 5A; Arias-Palomo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior structural work and shown in Figures 1 and 5A.

claim: Mutation of Phe146, Ser177, and Tyr179 blocks ssDNA binding and DNA-stimulated ATPase activity, as well as the loading of DnaB onto M13 DNA.
source: Mutation of these residues blocks ssDNA binding and DNA-stimulated ATPase activity, as well as the loading of DnaB onto M13 DNA (Arias-Palomo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Alteration of Phe146, Ser177, and Tyr179 interferes with the ability of DnaC to stimulate DNA unwinding by DnaB.
source: Their alteration also interferes with the ability of DnaC to stimulate DNA unwinding by DnaB (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Lys143 is a conserved residue positioned one helical turn upstream of Phe146 that is proximal to the substrate phosphodiester backbone in a subset of DnaC protomers.
source: In the course of our phylogenetic analyses of DnaC/I-family proteins, we noted another conserved residue, Lys143, that is positioned one helical turn upstream of Phe146 (Figures 1 and 5A). Inspection of the DnaBC•ssDNA structure shows that this amino acid is proximal to the substrate phosphodiester backbone in a subset of DnaC protomers, forming a small patch with its Phe146, Ser177, and Tyr179 counterparts that grasps the nucleic acid substrate (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and structural inspection shown in Figures 1, 5A, and 5B.

claim: Substitution of Lys143 with glutamic acid leads to a complete loss of DNA/DnaB-stimulated ATPase activity by DnaC and strongly impaired DNA binding.
source: Substitution of Lys143 with glutamic acid leads to a complete loss of DNA/DnaB-stimulated ATPase activity by DnaC and strongly impaired DNA binding (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The K143E mutant proved incapable of loading DnaB onto M13 DNA or activating DNA strand separation by the helicase.
source: The K143E mutant also proved incapable of loading DnaB onto M13 DNA or activating DNA strand separation by the helicase (Figure 5D–E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5D–E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: Lys143 is a part of the mechanism used by DnaC to sense ssDNA.
source: These findings demonstrate that, as with other conserved amino acids in its local neighborhood, Lys143 is a part of the mechanism used by DnaC to sense ssDNA.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing its role in DNA binding and function.

claim: The inability of a DnaCK143E mutant to facilitate DnaB loading onto ssDNA suggests that the alteration allows the loader to maintain a persistent, open-ring state of the helicase.
source: The inability of a DnaCK143E mutant to facilitate DnaB loading onto ssDNA—even though it has an intact HBD and stably binds DnaB—suggests that the alteration allows the loader to maintain a persistent, open-ring state of the helicase.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations about the K143E mutant.

claim: A second conserved element in DnaC/I-family proteins is the presence of an invariant arginine, Arg216, one helical turn upstream of the Arg-finger.
source: A second conserved element in DnaC/I-family proteins revealed by sequence homology is the presence of an invariant arginine, Arg216, one helical turn upstream of the Arg-finger (Figures 1 and 6A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figures 1 and 6A.

claim: The R216D mutant proved unable to hydrolyze ATP, did not stimulate DNA unwinding by DnaB, and could only support DnaB loading at a level comparable to the Sensor I mutant.
source: The R216D mutant proved unable to hydrolyze ATP, did not stimulate DNA unwinding by DnaB, and could only support DnaB loading at a level comparable to the Sensor I mutant (Figure 6B–D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6B–D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: DnaCR216A showed a moderate capacity to support helicase loading and stimulated DNA unwinding by DnaB with wild-type efficiency.
source: By contrast, DnaCR216A showed a moderate capacity to support helicase loading and stimulated DNA unwinding by DnaB with wild-type efficiency (Figure 6C–D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6C–D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: The R216A construct exhibited slightly higher ATPase activity than native DnaC and additionally required only DnaB (and not ssDNA) for ATPase function.
source: Surprisingly, the R216A construct actually exhibited slightly higher ATPase activity than native DnaC and additionally required only DnaB (and not ssDNA) for ATPase function (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The R216A mutant proved capable of counteracting the strong inhibitory block placed on DnaC ATPase activity in the context of a K143E substitution.
source: The alanine mutant also proved capable of counteracting the strong inhibitory block placed on DnaC ATPase activity in the context of a K143E substitution (Figure 6E), although it was unable to restore the activation of DNA unwinding by DnaB in such a context (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Arg216 is a key coupling element in DnaC, repressing nucleotide turnover in the presence of DnaB until ssDNA also associates with the complex.
source: These results reveal that Arg216 is as a key coupling element in DnaC, repressing nucleotide turnover in the presence of DnaB until ssDNA also associates with the complex.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data on R216 mutants.

claim: The dnaC810 mutation results from the substitution of Glu176 with glycine.
source: Numerous DnaC variants have been isolated as suppressors for the loss of critical replication restart proteins in genetic screens (Sandler et al., 1996); one is dnaC810, which results from the substitution of Glu176 with glycine.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior genetic work.

claim: Glu176 sits proximal to the DNA-binding residues Ser177 and Tyr179, in a loop adjoining the Walker-B element that undergoes a conformational switch between DNA-free and -bound states of DnaC.
source: We noted that Glu176, though not particularly well-conserved, sits proximal to the DNA-binding residues Ser177 and Tyr179, in a loop adjoining the Walker-B element that undergoes a conformational switch between DNA-free and -bound states of DnaC (Figure 1C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The E176G variant proved capable of supporting both DnaB loading and the activation of fork unwinding by the helicase, at levels only moderately decreased from native DnaC.
source: The variant proved capable of supporting both DnaB loading and the activation of fork unwinding by the helicase, at levels only moderately decreased from native DnaC (Figure 7A–B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7A–B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F–G.

claim: DnaCE176G was capable of supporting the ssDNA- and DnaB-dependent ATPase function of the loader, and the activity of the mutant loader exceeded that of wild-type protein by ~50%.
source: DnaCE176G was also capable of supporting the ssDNA- and DnaB-dependent ATPase function of the loader (Figure 7C); interestingly, the activity of the mutant loader exceeded that of wild-type protein by ~50%.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The E176G substitution allowed DnaC to hydrolyze ATP when bound to DnaB alone, although at approximately half the rate as when DNA was present.
source: In addition, the substitution allowed DnaC to hydrolyze ATP when bound to DnaB alone, although at approximately half the rate as when DNA was present.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Like the R216A (Arg-coupler) substitution, the mutation present in the dnac810 strain has gained the ability to act on DnaB in a DNA-independent manner.
source: These data demonstrate that, like the R216A (Arg-coupler) substitution (Figure 6B), the mutation present in the dnac810 strain has gained the ability to act on DnaB in a DNA-independent manner.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the behaviors of the two mutants.

claim: DnaCR216A displayed an even greater ability to stimulate DnaB-mediated unwinding of the SSB-bound substrate than DnaC810 when PriC was absent.
source: Interestingly, DnaCR216A displayed an even greater ability to stimulate DnaB-mediated unwinding of the SSB-bound substrate than DnaC810 when PriC was absent.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The Arg-coupler plays a role in preventing DnaC from activating DnaB unless restart factors are present.
source: These data demonstrate that the Arg-coupler plays a role in preventing DnaC from activating DnaB unless restart factors are present.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data on SSB-coated fork unwinding.

claim: The opening of the DnaB ring and its subsequent engagement with DNA can occur independently of ATP hydrolysis by DnaC.
source: The opening of the DnaB ring and its subsequent engagement with DNA can occur independently of ATP hydrolysis by DnaC (Figure 2), a finding in accord with previous data showing that neither ATP binding nor the DnaC ATPase domains are required for DnaB loading in vitro (Arias-Palomo et al., 2013; Davey et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 and citations to prior work.

claim: ATP turnover improves the efficiency of helicase loading.
source: However, ATP turnover does improve the efficiency of helicase loading (Figure 2), an observation in agreement both with early work of Wahles et al., 1988 (which reported that an ATP-hydrolysis step is important in the binding of the DnaBC complex to DNA) and with a study showing that the replication factor C (RFC) clamp loader becomes compromised for DNA binding when its D or E subunit bears a mutated Arg-finger (Johnson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 and citations to prior work.

claim: The ability to hydrolyze nucleotides has a potentiating effect on the capacity of DnaC to activate DNA unwinding by DnaB.
source: Interestingly, the ability to hydrolyze nucleotides also has a potentiating effect on the capacity of DnaC to activate DNA unwinding by DnaB (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Hydrolysis-defective DnaC mutants are less capable of activating DnaB than an ATP-binding (Walker-A, K112R) mutant.
source: Indeed, hydrolysis-defective DnaC mutants are less capable of activating DnaB than an ATP-binding (Walker-A, K112R) mutant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different mutants in Figure 4C.

claim: All ATPase mutants are substantially compromised for activating DNA unwinding compared to wild-type DnaC or the helicase-binding domain of DnaC alone.
source: Moreover, all ATPase mutants are substantially compromised for activating DNA unwinding compared to wild-type DnaC or the helicase-binding domain of DnaC alone.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The HBD is an independent helicase-activating element regulated by its associated ATPase module.
source: These observations indicate that the HBD is an independent helicase-activating element regulated by its associated ATPase module and that ATP turnover by the loader is important for allowing DnaB to shift into a translocation-competent form.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data comparing HBD and full-length DnaC activities.

claim: ATP turnover by the loader is important for allowing DnaB to shift into a translocation-competent form.
source: These observations indicate that the HBD is an independent helicase-activating element regulated by its associated ATPase module and that ATP turnover by the loader is important for allowing DnaB to shift into a translocation-competent form.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data on DnaC mutants and their effects on DnaB unwinding.

claim: Recent images of DNA-free and DNA-bound structures of the DnaBC complex have revealed that the nucleotide status of the helicase flips from an ADP state to an ATP configuration when DNA is present.
source: Recent images of DNA-free and DNA-bound structures of the DnaBC complex have revealed that the nucleotide status of the helicase flips from an ADP state to an ATP configuration when DNA is present (Arias-Palomo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior structural work.

claim: The ability of the helicase to interact productively with nucleotides impacts DNA loading.
source: In testing this idea with a double Walker-A/Walker-B (KAEA) mutant of DnaB, the ability of the helicase to interact productively with nucleotides indeed impacts DNA loading (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A role for nucleotide turnover by DnaB is reminiscent of the need for ATP by the eukaryotic Mcm2-7 replicative helicase to support its loading onto DNA by the origin recognition complex (ORC).
source: Although this coupling is not a strict dependency, a role for nucleotide turnover by DnaB is reminiscent of the need for ATP by the eukaryotic Mcm2-7 replicative helicase to support its loading onto DNA by the origin recognition complex (ORC) (Coster et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work supported by a citation.

claim: In eukaryotes, unloading of the Cdc45/Mcm2-7/GINS helicase is facilitated by ubiquitylation of MCM7 and removal of the CMG helicase by CDC48/p97.
source: In contrast to eukaryotes, where unloading of the Cdc45/Mcm2-7/GINS helicase is facilitated by ubiquitylation of MCM7 and removal of the CMG helicase by CDC48/p97 (Deng et al., 2019), relatively little is known about how DnaB helicases are removed from DNA following replication termination in bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on eukaryotic helicase unloading.

claim: Relatively little is known about how DnaB helicases are removed from DNA following replication termination in bacteria.
source: In contrast to eukaryotes, where unloading of the Cdc45/Mcm2-7/GINS helicase is facilitated by ubiquitylation of MCM7 and removal of the CMG helicase by CDC48/p97 (Deng et al., 2019), relatively little is known about how DnaB helicases are removed from DNA following replication termination in bacteria.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A prior genetic screen noted that the integrity of Lys143 is important for E. coli viability.
source: Lys143 is generally a lysine or arginine in DnaC/DnaI homologs, and a prior genetic screen Hupert-Kocurek et al., 2007 noted that the integrity of this residue is important for E. coli viability.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior genetic work.

claim: Disruption of Lys143 and other amino acids in the DNA-binding region block DNA binding.
source: Biochemical studies show that disruption of this residue and other amino acids in the region block DNA binding (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C; Arias-Palomo et al., 2019), thereby short-circuiting the ability of the nucleic acid substrate to stimulate ATP hydrolysis by DnaC when the loader is bound to DnaB.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and a citation.

claim: The integrity of the DNA-binding patch on DnaC supports the ability of ssDNA to activate all known DnaC functions, even though it is situated over 20 Å away from the DnaC ATPase center.
source: Overall, the integrity of the DNA-binding patch on DnaC supports the ability of ssDNA to activate all known DnaC functions, even though it is situated over 20 Å away from the DnaC ATPase center.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data and structural information.

claim: E. coli DnaC is a monomer on its own and forms stable oligomeric interactions only when templated by a pre-existing DnaB hexamer.
source: Unlike a majority of AAA+ ATPases, E. coli DnaC is a monomer on its own (Galletto et al., 2004b) and forms stable oligomeric interactions only when templated by a pre-existing DnaB hexamer (Kobori and Kornberg, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior biochemical work.

claim: Formation of a higher-order oligomer state is generally a prerequisite for AAA+ ATPase function, as the active site of one subunit typically depends on the contribution of an arginine or lysine from a partner subunit to support nucleotide turnover.
source: Formation of a higher-order oligomer state is generally a prerequisite for AAA+ ATPase function, as the active site of one subunit typically depends on the contribution of an arginine or lysine from a partner subunit to support nucleotide turnover (Neuwald, 1999a; Neuwald et al., 1999b).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AAA+ ATPases supported by citations.

claim: Mutation of the Arg-finger residue to alanine in E. coli DnaC does not interfere with the ability of the loader to deliver DnaB to oriC, but does interfere with DnaC-dependent DNA replication in vitro and DnaC function in vivo.
source: Prior work has shown that mutation of the so-termed 'Arg-finger' residue to alanine in E. coli DnaC does not interfere with the ability of the loader to deliver DnaB to oriC, but does interfere with DnaC-dependent DNA replication in vitro and DnaC function in vivo (Makowska-Grzyska and Kaguni, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Arg-finger is critical for DnaC ATPase activity.
source: Here we have shown that this amino acid is critical for DnaC ATPase activity (Figure 2A) and that while it is only moderately important for DnaB loading, its presence is necessary to activate DNA unwinding by the helicase (Figures 2D and 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A, 2D, and 4C.

claim: The integrity of Arg216 is unnecessary for DnaC to bind ATP or associate with DnaB but is important for supporting replication in vitro and for cell viability.
source: Prior studies have shown that the integrity of this residue is unnecessary for DnaC to bind ATP or associate with DnaB but is important for supporting replication in vitro and for cell viability (Makowska-Grzyska and Kaguni, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Arg216 is an essential element for coupling substrate DNA binding to loader ATPase activity.
source: Here, we have shown that Arg216 is actually an essential element for coupling substrate DNA binding to loader ATPase activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data on R216 mutants.

claim: Inspection of a DNA-free DnaBC structure reveals that Arg216 is positioned where the nucleophilic water would be expected to reside prior to ATP hydrolysis; in the presence of ssDNA, this amino acid shifts away to allow access to the reactive γ-PO4.
source: Inspection of a DNA-free DnaBC structure reveals that Arg216 is positioned where the nucleophilic water would be expected to reside prior to ATP hydrolysis; in the presence of ssDNA, this amino acid shifts away to allow access to the reactive γ-PO4 (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 8A–B.

claim: Arg216 acts not just as a substrate/ATPase coupler, but also as a steric governor, preventing the DnaC ATPase from firing when oligomerized by DnaB to prevent futile cycling until substrate DNA is bound.
source: Thus, Arg216 acts not just as a substrate/ATPase coupler, but also as a steric governor, preventing the DnaC ATPase from firing when oligomerized by DnaB to prevent futile cycling until substrate DNA is bound.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural and biochemical data on Arg216.

claim: The action of the Arg-coupler explains how the ATPase activity of DnaC allosterically responds to the binding of ssDNA at a region distal to the active site.
source: The action of the Arg-coupler explains how the ATPase activity of DnaC allosterically responds to the binding of ssDNA at a region distal to the active site.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural and biochemical data.

claim: The binding of ssDNA to the tetrad residues elicits a subtle rocking and compression motion between neighboring DnaC protomers, which leads the Arg-coupler to shift out of the active site, releasing its repressive action on ATPase function.
source: The binding of ssDNA to the tetrad residues elicits a subtle rocking and compression motion between neighboring DnaC protomers (Arias-Palomo et al., 2019); this action leads the Arg-coupler to shift out of the active site, releasing its repressive action on ATPase function (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and a citation to prior work.

claim: The Arg-coupler acts in a manner akin to the 'glutamate switch', a residue found in many AAA+ ATPases that controls the conformation of the catalytic glutamate in response to ligand binding.
source: In this regard, the Arg-coupler acts in a manner akin to the 'glutamate switch', a residue found in many AAA+ ATPases that controls the conformation of the catalytic glutamate in response to ligand binding (Zhang and Wigley, 2008).
evidence: This is a comparison to a known mechanism in other AAA+ ATPases, supported by a citation.

claim: A polar amino acid at the position of the glutamate switch is present in E. coli DnaC (Thr134), but it does not make ideal hydrogen-bonding interactions with the catalytic glutamate (Glu170) in the repressed (DNA-free) ATPase state.
source: Interestingly, a polar amino acid at the position of the glutamate switch is present in E. coli DnaC (Thr134), but it does not make ideal hydrogen-bonding interactions with the catalytic glutamate (Glu170) in the repressed (DNA-free) ATPase state (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Thr134 forms a contact with an acidic amino acid (Asp 189), which is in turn hydrogen-bonded to the Arg-finger.
source: Instead, Thr134 forms a contact with an acidic amino acid (Asp 189), which is in turn hydrogen-bonded to the Arg-finger.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Neither the glutamate switch threonine nor its acidic anchor residue is particularly well conserved among DnaC/DnaI homologs, although these two amino-acid positions are typically occupied by polar residues.
source: Neither the glutamate switch threonine nor its acidic anchor residue is particularly well conserved among DnaC/DnaI homologs, although these two amino-acid positions are typically occupied by polar residues (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Purified DnaC810 has been shown to load DnaB on SSB-coated ssDNA and on D-loops, bypassing the need for the PriA replication restart protein.
source: Purified DnaC810 has been shown to load DnaB on SSB-coated ssDNA and on D-loops, bypassing the need for the PriA replication restart protein, and it has been proposed that the DnaB loading activity of this mutant is mediated by a cryptic DNA-binding site in DnaC (Xu and Marians, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Glu176 sits on a loop that connects one-half of the DNA-binding tetrad (Ser177 and Tyr179) to the Walker-B loop of the ATPase center.
source: Inspection of the structure shows that Glu176 sits on a loop that connects one-half of the DNA-binding tetrad (Ser177 and Tyr179) to the Walker-B loop of the ATPase center (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DnaC810 shows a similar pattern of behavior as the alanine substitution of Arg216: DnaB-dependent but ssDNA-independent ATPase activity, and near wild-type efficiency in loading DnaB onto DNA and activating the helicase for fork unwinding.
source: Interestingly, DnaC810 shows a similar pattern of behavior as the alanine substitution of Arg216: DnaB-dependent but ssDNA-independent ATPase activity, and near wild-type efficiency in loading DnaB onto DNA and activating the helicase for fork unwinding (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Unlike the R216A mutant, the dnaC810 allele supports cell viability.
source: However, unlike the R216A mutant, the dnaC810 allele supports cell viability (Makowska-Grzyska and Kaguni, 2010; Sandler et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A comparison of structures of the DnaBC complex in DNA-free and -bound states shows that the Walker-B loop on which Glu176 sits switches between two conformations.
source: A comparison of structures of the DnaBC complex in DNA-free and -bound states shows that the Walker-B loop on which Glu176 sits switches between two conformations (Arias-Palomo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior structural work.

claim: The substitution of glutamic acid with glycine in DnaC810 likely alters the flexibility of the Walker-B region, perhaps mimicking a DNA-bound conformational state to relieve DnaC of the repressive action of Arg216.
source: Although a structure of DnaC810 bound to DnaB is currently unavailable, it seems likely that the substitution of the glutamic acid with glycine alters the flexibility of the Walker-B region, perhaps mimicking a DNA-bound conformational state to relieve DnaC of the repressive action of Arg216.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: The finding that the DnaC810 can act in a manner similar to that of the arginine-coupler mutant suggests that tight ATPase control by the loader is necessary to properly coordinate its activity with pathways that resuscitate stalled replication forks.
source: The finding that the DnaC810 can act in a manner similar to that of the arginine-coupler mutant suggests that tight ATPase control by the loader is necessary to properly coordinate its activity with pathways that resuscitate stalled replication forks.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data on DnaC810 and R216A mutants.

claim: DnaA, a DnaC paralog that serves to reorganize and melt origins to initiate replication in bacteria, retains a highly conserved arginine in the same position as the Arg-coupler.
source: However, DnaA, a DnaC paralog that serves to reorganize and melt origins to initiate replication in bacteria, does retain a highly conserved arginine in the same position as the Arg-coupler.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis.

claim: Sequence analyses show that two proteins used to catalyze replicative helicase loading in eukaryotes, Orc4 and Orc1, also retain an element analogous to the Arg-coupler.
source: Sequence analyses show that two proteins used to catalyze replicative helicase loading in eukaryotes, Orc4 and Orc1, also retain such an element (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: DnaA, Orc4, and Orc1 all belong to the same 'initiator' subgroup, or clade, of AAA+ proteins.
source: Interestingly, these proteins all belong to the same 'initiator' subgroup, or clade, of AAA+ proteins, suggesting that the coupling arginine seen in DnaC may play a similar role in regulating substrate-dependent ATP turnover in these proteins as well.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic classification of AAA+ proteins.

claim: The coupling arginine seen in DnaC may play a similar role in regulating substrate-dependent ATP turnover in DnaA, Orc4, and Orc1.
source: Interestingly, these proteins all belong to the same 'initiator' subgroup, or clade, of AAA+ proteins, suggesting that the coupling arginine seen in DnaC may play a similar role in regulating substrate-dependent ATP turnover in these proteins as well.
evidence: This is speculation based on sequence conservation and functional similarity.

claim: The equivalent of DnaC-Arg216 in E. coli DnaA (Arg281) is dispensable for ATP binding and melting of oriC DNA, but necessary for forming a sufficiently stable complex that can support DnaB loading by DnaC.
source: In the case of DnaA, the integrity of the equivalent of DnaC-Arg216 (Arg281 in E. coli DnaA) has been shown to be dispensable for ATP binding and melting of oriC DNA, but necessary for forming a sufficiently stable complex that can support DnaB loading by DnaC (Felczak and Kaguni, 2004); by comparison, mutation of the neighboring Arg-finger of DnaA, R285A, leads to a failure in unwinding oriC (Kawakami et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on DnaA.

claim: Mutation of the neighboring Arg-finger of DnaA, R285A, leads to a failure in unwinding oriC.
source: In the case of DnaA, the integrity of the equivalent of DnaC-Arg216 (Arg281 in E. coli DnaA) has been shown to be dispensable for ATP binding and melting of oriC DNA, but necessary for forming a sufficiently stable complex that can support DnaB loading by DnaC (Felczak and Kaguni, 2004); by comparison, mutation of the neighboring Arg-finger of DnaA, R285A, leads to a failure in unwinding oriC (Kawakami et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on DnaA.

claim: Mutation of the analogous residue to the Arg-coupler in human Orc1 (Arg666, to Trp) has been linked to Meier-Gorlin syndrome.
source: Interestingly, although there is no known data on the phenotypic effect of mutating the equivalent residue in human Orc4 (Arg205), mutation of the analogous residue in Orc1 (Arg666, to Trp) has been linked to Meier-Gorlin syndrome (Guernsey et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on human Orc1.

claim: IstB does not possess a clear homolog of the Arg-coupler.
source: Other proteins in the initiator clade, such as IstB (a transposition helper protein and another DnaC paralog), do not possess a clear homolog of the Arg-coupler, nor do several archetypal AAA+ ATPases of other clades (e.g., clamp loader, classic, pre-Sensor I insert, etc).
evidence: This is based on sequence and structural analysis.

claim: In addition to blocking access to the reactive γ-PO4 of bound nucleotide, the Arg-coupler of DnaB-bound DnaC also engages the polar Sensor I amino acid and releases this interaction when DNA is bound.
source: In addition to blocking access to the reactive γ-PO4 of bound nucleotide, the Arg-coupler of DnaB-bound DnaC also engages the polar Sensor I amino acid (Figure 8D) and releases this interaction when DNA is bound.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The Sensor I amino acid is a conserved feature of AAA+ proteins and is generally important for ATP hydrolysis.
source: The Sensor I amino acid is a conserved feature of AAA+ proteins and is generally important for ATP hydrolysis (Hattendorf and Lindquist, 2002; Neuwald et al., 1999b; Steel et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AAA+ proteins supported by citations.

claim: In IstB, whose ATPase is primed by DNA binding but not actuated until it engages its client IstA transposase, the Arg-coupler is replaced with a small amino acid (e.g., alanine), but a bulky amino acid (tyrosine) on the Walker-B loop occupies the same general position to occlude the γ-PO4 moiety and remodel the Sensor I loop.
source: In the case of IstB— whose ATPase is primed by DNA binding but not actuated until it engages its client IstA transposase—a DNA-bound structure of the protein shows that the Arg-coupler is replaced with a small amino acid (e.g., alanine), but that a bulky amino acid (tyrosine) on the Walker-B loop occupies the same general position to occlude the γ-PO4 moiety and remodel the Sensor I loop (Figure 8E; Arias-Palomo and Berger, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 8E and a citation.

claim: Clamp loaders lack the upstream Arg-coupler; however, in the presence of a client clamp, access to the γ-PO4 is occluded by a Sensor I interaction with a positively charged residue on an adjacent helix.
source: Clamp loaders, whose AAA+ clade is closely related to that of the initiators, also lack the upstream Arg-coupler; however, in the presence of a client clamp—which is necessary but insufficient for stimulating ATPase activity on its own—access to the γ-PO4 is again occluded by a Sensor I interaction with a positively charged residue on an adjacent helix (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 8F.

claim: A comparison of clamp loader structures reveals that an arginine or lysine in a highly conserved central helix can, upon DNA binding, swing out to release the Sensor I residue, thereby allowing the Arg-finger to access the γ-PO4.
source: A comparison of clamp loader structures reveals that an arginine or lysine in this highly conserved central helix can, upon DNA binding, swing out to release the Sensor I residue, thereby allowing the Arg-finger to access the γ-PO4 (Bowman et al., 2004; Gaubitz et al., 2020; Simonetta et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural work on clamp loaders.

claim: An N-terminal motif known as 'RFC box II' has been shown in the archaeal clamp loader system to be important for linking ATP hydrolysis to clamp loading: when ablated, the loader shows elevated ATPase activity but is compromised for clamp loading, a behavior similar to that of the DnaC Arg-coupler.
source: Interestingly, an N-terminal motif known as 'RFC box II' also has been shown in the archaeal clamp loader system to be important for linking ATP hydrolysis to clamp loading: when ablated, the loader shows elevated ATPase activity but is compromised for clamp loading, a behavior similar to that of the DnaC Arg-coupler (Seybert et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on archaeal clamp loaders.

claim: An interesting distinction of initiators and clamp/helicase/transposase loaders compared to other AAA+ systems is that they are switch-like in their behavior, as opposed to acting in a more processive manner.
source: An interesting distinction of initiators and clamp/helicase/transposase loaders compared to other AAA+ systems is that they are switch-like in their behavior, as opposed to acting in a more processive manner.
evidence: This is a characterization based on known behaviors of these protein classes.

claim: Restricting access to γ-PO4 of ATP and sequestering the Sensor I amino acid may serve as a general fail-safe in switch-like AAA+ systems to allow an active ATPase center to be assembled while avoiding premature hydrolytic events.
source: Restricting access to γ-PO4 of ATP and sequestering the Sensor I amino acid may thus serve as a general fail-safe in these systems, as it does in DnaC, to allow an active ATPase center to be assembled while avoiding premature hydrolytic events.
evidence: This is speculation based on the comparative analysis of different AAA+ systems.
